Well... it's just like I was saying a minute ago, doctor. I keep telling my daughter, I keep telling the pastor, but they just look at me with pity and they don't understand the reality of it. I am the reason my friend passed away. It's a terrible, heavy burden, but it's the absolute truth. At my age, standing on that hard linoleum all day... well, the rubber mats they give us don't do a lick of good, and my ankles just swell up like balloons by the end of my shift. So I was sitting in my armchair, and I saw her name pop up on the caller ID, and I just... I ignored it. I deliberately ignored my dear friend. 

And it wasn't just that I didn't call her back. It's what was in my heart. I sat there and I let these selfish, ugly thoughts just fester in my mind. I remember thinking, 'I just want everyone to leave me be, I wish people would stop bothering me.' Just wicked, wicked thoughts. And then... then she was gone. God took her because of my wickedness. He heard what was in my mind, and He acted on it. A person whose own selfishness kills their friend... that is a rotten person. There's no other word for it. It's like a rot inside an apple, you know? You might not see it right away on the outside, but it ruins the whole bushel. 

And now... now it's not just her. I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church because of me. I see it happening every single Sunday. Last week, Mary Peters was coughing so badly she had to leave the service, and the week before that, the youth group van broke down on the highway. People are losing their jobs, they're getting sick, and they don't realize it's because I'm sitting right there in the third pew, bringing all this sin and filth into His house. I shouldn't even be allowed in the sanctuary anymore. I'm a blight on all those good people, and bringing me to a clinic isn't going to wash that rot out of my soul.

Well, they wouldn't say it out loud to me, of course. People are too polite for that, especially at our church. We've been going to First Presbyterian since my daughter was just a little thing in pigtails, so they know me. Well... no, doctor. No, I don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I know you're trying to help, and my daughter says the same thing. She tells me, 'Mom, you're just grieving, you're just tired from work.' And I am tired, I won't deny that. Working the register at seventy-four is no picnic, let me tell you. He's looking right out, and his voice changes just a fraction, and I know he's warning me. He's letting me know that God has marked me. He has to do it from the pulpit because, well, how do you pull an old widow aside and tell her she's destroying the church? 

And the choir... oh, the choir. It's so beautiful, usually. Mrs. Higgins directs them, she used to teach music at the middle school before she retired. But now, when they sing certain lines... like last week, that hymn about bearing our sins and griefs. They know that the church is suffering, that Mary Peters is sick and the van broke down and all these terrible things are happening, because I brought this on us. I brought this rot into the sanctuary. So, no, doctor. It's not possible that I'm mistaken. The signs are everywhere, and they are all pointing right at me. God has marked me for what I did to my friend, and everyone at church knows it.

Well... I don't know if "unable to stop" is the right way to put it. I'm not really trying to stop them, doctor. Like I said before, I'm not trying to push them away or focus on other things. I mean, how can you stop thinking about something that's just... the truth? It's not like a song stuck in your head, you know? It's not like that. 

These thoughts... they're just my reality now. They're just there. When I wake up in the morning, and my joints are all stiff, and I have to sit on the edge of the bed for a good ten minutes just rubbing my knees before I can even stand up to go make my tea... the thoughts are there. And when I'm making my tea—I always have Earl Grey, with just a little splash of milk, the way my husband used to like it before he passed, God rest his soul—I'm not standing there thinking, "Oh, I wish I could stop thinking about what I did to my friend." I'm just... existing with it. It's like a heavy wet blanket I'm wearing all the time. 

So I don't know if I'm "unable" to stop, because I don't think I'm trying to stop. I deserve to feel this way. I deserve the weight of it. Why would I try to stop thinking about it when it's my punishment? It's what God wants for me, clearly. That's why He marked me. That's why Pastor Miller looks at me the way he does. You don't just turn off a punishment from God because it's uncomfortable. You bear it. You just... bear it. So, no, I don't feel like I'm trying to stop and failing. I just... I just let them be there, because they have to be.

Other things? Well... no. No, doctor, there isn't really room in my head for anything else, because this... this takes up every waking moment. I don't know why I would feel guilty about, oh, leaving the porch light on or forgetting to water the geraniums, when I have this terrible, crushing weight on my soul.

I am the reason she died. \n\nShe called me, you see, and I was just so tired after standing at the grocery register all day, my feet were aching so badly, so I didn't call her back. I just didn't pick up the phone to call her back. And worse than that, I... I had ugly thoughts sometimes. Just wicked, ugly thoughts that I let into my mind, and I know that's why she was taken. Because of me. My thoughts did it. \n\nAnd it’s not just her, it's spreading, I can see it happening. I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church because of me. The whole congregation is suffering, people are having hard times and getting sick, and it's because I'm sitting right there in the pews with all this sin and ugliness inside me. I keep trying to explain to my daughter and the pastor that God is punishing everyone for my thoughts, and that I'm just a terrible, rotten person, but they wouldn't listen and they just made me come here to talk to you. But a doctor can't fix what I've done. I ruined everything. I'm the reason for all of it.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what you mean when you say you're a 'terrible, rotten person'?\n\nPatient: Well... it's just like I was saying a minute ago, doctor. I keep telling my daughter, I keep telling the pastor, but they just look at me with pity and they don't understand the reality of it. I am the reason my friend passed away. It's a terrible, heavy burden, but it's the absolute truth. She called me that Tuesday afternoon, and I had been on my feet for almost nine hours at the register. At my age, standing on that hard linoleum all day... well, the rubber mats they give us don't do a lick of good, and my ankles just swell up like balloons by the end of my shift. So I was sitting in my armchair, and I saw her name pop up on the caller ID, and I just... I ignored it. I deliberately ignored my dear friend. \n\nAnd it wasn't just that I didn't call her back. It's what was in my heart. I sat there and I let these selfish, ugly thoughts just fester in my mind. I remember thinking, 'I just want everyone to leave me be, I wish people would stop bothering me.' Just wicked, wicked thoughts. And then... then she was gone. God took her because of my wickedness. He heard what was in my mind, and He acted on it. A person whose own selfishness kills their friend... that is a rotten person. There's no other word for it. It's like a rot inside an apple, you know? You might not see it right away on the outside, but it ruins the whole bushel. \n\nAnd now... now it's not just her. I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church because of me. I see it happening every single Sunday. Last week, Mary Peters was coughing so badly she had to leave the service, and the week before that, the youth group van broke down on the highway. People are losing their jobs, they're getting sick, and they don't realize it's because I'm sitting right there in the third pew, bringing all this sin and filth into His house. I shouldn't even be allowed in the sanctuary anymore. I'm a blight on all those good people, and bringing me to a clinic isn't going to wash that rot out of my soul.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself constantly thinking about these ugly thoughts, even when you try to focus on something else?\n\nPatient: I don't... I'm not exactly sure what you mean by trying to focus on something else. I haven't really noticed if I try to do that. I mean... what else is there to focus on now? \n\nI just go about my day, I suppose. Like yesterday, I was at work, standing at register four—they usually put me at register four because it's closer to the manager's booth and away from the draft of the sliding doors, which is good for my joints. And I'm just scanning things. A can of peaches, a box of cereal, a bunch of bananas. I just watch my wrinkled old hands dragging the barcodes across the glass, waiting for the red light and the beep. Beep, beep, beep. And I just... I don't know if I'm actively thinking about the ugly thoughts right in that exact second, or if they're just sitting there heavy in my chest like a stone. I don't think I'm trying to push them away or focus on the bananas, if that makes sense. I just stand there. \n\nAnd then a customer will get upset with me because their coupons didn't scan right, or because they have to pay ten cents for a bag now—people get so angry about that ten-cent charge, they really do, they yell right in your face—and they snap at me. And I just let them snap. I just nod and take it, because I know I deserve it for what I did to my friend. I deserve every bit of anger they have. But as far as constantly thinking about the thoughts or trying to distract myself with other things... I really couldn't say for sure. I just don't know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think other people believe that your thoughts can cause bad things to happen to others?\n\nPatient: Well, they wouldn't say it out loud to me, of course. People are too polite for that, especially at our church. We've been going to First Presbyterian since my daughter was just a little thing in pigtails, so they know me. They know I'm a widow and I work hard, so they smile and they hand me the bulletin on Sunday mornings. But... but I know they know. I can see it. I can feel it. \n\nThey know my thoughts are causing all this misery. It's so clear to me during the service. When Pastor Miller stands up there at the pulpit—he's a good man, Pastor Miller, he's been with us for about twelve years now, came all the way from a parish in Ohio—when he says the prayers, he looks right out over the congregation, but I know he's looking at me. And the words he chooses... he'll talk about repenting for hidden sins, or the weight of a guilty conscience, and I just know. I know he's warning me. He's telling me that God has marked me. \n\nAnd the choir, too. Last week they sang 'Lord, Who Throughout These Forty Days,' and when they got to the part about 'our sins and griefs to bear,' the sopranos... they just held that note, and I could feel it piercing right through me. It wasn't just a hymn, doctor. It was a message. They were singing those certain lines to let me know that they understand why Mary Peters is sick, and why the van broke down, and why the church is suffering. They know I brought this on us. They're just too polite to ask me to leave the sanctuary, but they are warning me. They know I'm marked by God for what I did to my friend, and they know my thoughts are poisoning everything around me. They absolutely know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your thoughts might not be the cause of the bad things happening to others?\n\nPatient: Well... no, doctor. No, I don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I know you're trying to help, and my daughter says the same thing. She tells me, 'Mom, you're just grieving, you're just tired from work.' And I am tired, I won't deny that. Working the register at seventy-four is no picnic, let me tell you. My hands ache so much by the time I get home that I can barely open a jar of applesauce for my dinner. But being tired doesn't make you blind to the truth. \n\nI see the truth every Sunday. It's not just a feeling I have in my head, it's right there in front of me. When Pastor Miller stands up at the pulpit... I told you about this, he's such a good man, but he has a responsibility to his flock. When he says those prayers, when he talks about the weight of sin and the consequences of a hardened heart... he's not just speaking generally to the congregation. He's looking right out, and his voice changes just a fraction, and I know he's warning me. He's letting me know that God has marked me. He has to do it from the pulpit because, well, how do you pull an old widow aside and tell her she's destroying the church? \n\nAnd the choir... oh, the choir. It's so beautiful, usually. Mrs. Higgins directs them, she used to teach music at the middle school before she retired. But now, when they sing certain lines... like last week, that hymn about bearing our sins and griefs. The way they held those notes, the way the sopranos' voices just swelled up on those specific words... it was a message. It was a direct message to me. They were warning me, just like the pastor. They know that the church is suffering, that Mary Peters is sick and the van broke down and all these terrible things are happening, because I brought this on us. I brought this rot into the sanctuary. So, no, doctor. It's not possible that I'm mistaken. The signs are everywhere, and they are all pointing right at me. God has marked me for what I did to my friend, and everyone at church knows it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to stop thinking about these ugly thoughts, even when you want to?\n\nPatient: Well... Other people? You mean, do other people think their own thoughts cause harm? Well... I suppose I don't really know what goes on in anyone else's head, doctor. I only know what's in mine, and... well, I know what they believe about me. I don't know if Mrs. Gable or anyone else sitting in the pews thinks they have this awful, destructive power inside them. But I know for an absolute fact that they believe *my* thoughts did this. I know that they know. 

Like I was trying to explain to you a few minutes ago about the Sunday services... it's not just my imagination. When Pastor Miller is up there at the altar, and he bows his head and says the prayers for the sick and the afflicted, or when he asks the Lord to cleanse the congregation of hidden wickedness... I know he's talking directly to me. And the choir, when they sing those certain lines about facing judgment or bearing the weight of our transgressions... it's all coordinated. I know they are really warning me. They're trying to tell me, in the only way they can during a holy service, that they know God has marked me. 

It's just so heavy, sitting there in my usual spot—third row from the back, on the aisle, where I've sat since my husband was alive—holding my little paper bulletin and just feeling it all wash over me. The whole church is suffering right now, and they know exactly why. They know I brought this on us. They know the sickness and the bad luck came from the rot I let into my heart. So I really couldn't tell you if anyone else thinks their own mind can do this, but they certainly know mine did. They're just too polite, or maybe too frightened of the mark God put on me, to come right out and say it to my face during coffee hour in the fellowship hall. So they do it through the prayers and the hymns instead. They warn me. And I just have to sit there and listen to it, because they're right.

Beep, beep, beep. And I just... I don't know if I'm actively thinking about the ugly thoughts right in that exact second, or if they're just sitting there heavy in my chest like a stone. I don't think I'm trying to push them away or focus on the bananas, if that makes sense. I just stand there. \n\nAnd then a customer will get upset with me because their coupons didn't scan right, or because they have to pay ten cents for a bag now—people get so angry about that ten-cent charge, they really do, they yell right in your face—and they snap at me. And I just let them snap. I just nod and take it, because I know I deserve it for what I did to my friend. I deserve every bit of anger they have. But as far as constantly thinking about the thoughts or trying to distract myself with other things... I really couldn't say for sure. I just don't know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think other people believe that your thoughts can cause bad things to happen to others?\n\nPatient: Well, they wouldn't say it out loud to me, of course. People are too polite for that, especially at our church. We've been going to First Presbyterian since my daughter was just a little thing in pigtails, so they know me. They know I'm a widow and I work hard, so they smile and they hand me the bulletin on Sunday mornings. But... but I know they know. I can see it. I can feel it. \n\nThey know my thoughts are causing all this misery. It's so clear to me during the service. When Pastor Miller stands up there at the pulpit—he's a good man, Pastor Miller, he's been with us for about twelve years now, came all the way from a parish in Ohio—when he says the prayers, he looks right out over the congregation, but I know he's looking at me. And the words he chooses... he'll talk about repenting for hidden sins, or the weight of a guilty conscience, and I just know. I know he's warning me. He's telling me that God has marked me. \n\nAnd the choir, too. Last week they sang 'Lord, Who Throughout These Forty Days,' and when they got to the part about 'our sins and griefs to bear,' the sopranos... they just held that note, and I could feel it piercing right through me. It wasn't just a hymn, doctor. It was a message. They were singing those certain lines to let me know that they understand why Mary Peters is sick, and why the van broke down, and why the church is suffering. They know I brought this on us. They're just too polite to ask me to leave the sanctuary, but they are warning me. They know I'm marked by God for what I did to my friend, and they know my thoughts are poisoning everything around me. They absolutely know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your thoughts might not be the cause of the bad things happening to others?\n\nPatient: Well... no, doctor. No, I don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I know you're trying to help, and my daughter says the same thing. She tells me, 'Mom, you're just grieving, you're just tired from work.' And I am tired, I won't deny that. Working the register at seventy-four is no picnic, let me tell you. My hands ache so much by the time I get home that I can barely open a jar of applesauce for my dinner. But being tired doesn't make you blind to the truth. \n\nI see the truth every Sunday. It's not just a feeling I have in my head, it's right there in front of me. When Pastor Miller stands up at the pulpit... I told you about this, he's such a good man, but he has a responsibility to his flock. When he says those prayers, when he talks about the weight of sin and the consequences of a hardened heart... he's not just speaking generally to the congregation. He's looking right out, and his voice changes just a fraction, and I know he's warning me. He's letting me know that God has marked me. He has to do it from the pulpit because, well, how do you pull an old widow aside and tell her she's destroying the church? \n\nAnd the choir... oh, the choir. It's so beautiful, usually. Mrs. Higgins directs them, she used to teach music at the middle school before she retired. But now, when they sing certain lines... like last week, that hymn about bearing our sins and griefs. The way they held those notes, the way the sopranos' voices just swelled up on those specific words... it was a message. It was a direct message to me. They were warning me, just like the pastor. They know that the church is suffering, that Mary Peters is sick and the van broke down and all these terrible things are happening, because I brought this on us. I brought this rot into the sanctuary. So, no, doctor. It's not possible that I'm mistaken. The signs are everywhere, and they are all pointing right at me. God has marked me for what I did to my friend, and everyone at church knows it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to stop thinking about these ugly thoughts, even when you want to?\n\nPatient: Well... I don't know if \"unable to stop\" is the right way to put it. I'm not really trying to stop them, doctor. Like I said before, I'm not trying to push them away or focus on other things. I mean, how can you stop thinking about something that's just... the truth? It's not like a song stuck in your head, you know? Like when they play those jingles on the radio at the grocery store—they play the same six songs on a loop all day long, and sometimes you just want to turn it off, but you can't. It's not like that. \n\nThese thoughts... they're just my reality now. They're just there. When I wake up in the morning, and my joints are all stiff, and I have to sit on the edge of the bed for a good ten minutes just rubbing my knees before I can even stand up to go make my tea... the thoughts are there. And when I'm making my tea—I always have Earl Grey, with just a little splash of milk, the way my husband used to like it before he passed, God rest his soul—I'm not standing there thinking, \"Oh, I wish I could stop thinking about what I did to my friend.\" I'm just... existing with it. It's like a heavy wet blanket I'm wearing all the time. \n\nSo I don't know if I'm \"unable\" to stop, because I don't think I'm trying to stop. I deserve to feel this way. I deserve the weight of it. Why would I try to stop thinking about it when it's my punishment? It's what God wants for me, clearly. That's why He marked me. That's why Pastor Miller looks at me the way he does. You don't just turn off a punishment from God because it's uncomfortable. You bear it. You just... bear it. So, no, I don't feel like I'm trying to stop and failing. I just... I just let them be there, because they have to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty or ashamed about things that have nothing to do with your friend's death or the church?\n\nPatient: Other things? Well... no. No, doctor, there isn't really room in my head for anything else, because this... this takes up every waking moment. I don't know why I would feel guilty about, oh, leaving the porch light on or forgetting to water the geraniums, when I have this terrible, crushing weight on my soul. \n\nI keep telling them—I tell my daughter, I even tried to tell Mrs. Higgins after service one day, though of course she already knew—I keep telling them that I'm the reason my friend died. It's just a fact, plain as day. She called me, you see, and I was just so tired from standing on my feet all day at the store, scanning barcodes and bagging groceries until my shoulders ached, and I just... I didn't call her back. I looked right at the phone and I didn't pick it up. And I had these ugly thoughts sometimes, just terrible, selfish thoughts because I was tired and I didn't want to hear her complain about her hip again. Just ugly, ugly thoughts inside my head. \n\nAnd then she was gone. And you can't undo that, doctor. You can't just apologize to a gravestone and expect it to wipe the slate clean. God sees what's in your heart. And because of that, because of the rot I let into my soul, I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church. He's punishing the whole congregation because of me. The sickness, the trouble they've been having... it's all flowing out from what I did, from those ugly thoughts and that phone call I never made. So, no, I don't feel ashamed about other little everyday things. How could I even think about anything else, when I know I've brought all this misery down on everyone's heads?\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else believes that their thoughts can cause bad things to happen to others in the same way you do?\n\nPatient: Other people? You mean, do other people think their own thoughts cause harm? Well... I suppose I don't really know what goes on in anyone else's head, doctor. I only know what's in mine, and... well, I know what they believe about me. I don't know if Mrs. Gable or anyone else sitting in the pews thinks they have this awful, destructive power inside them. But I know for an absolute fact that they believe *my* thoughts did this. I know that they know. \n\nLike I was trying to explain to you a few minutes ago about the Sunday services... it's not just my imagination. When Pastor Miller is up there at the altar, and he bows his head and says the prayers for the sick and the afflicted, or when he asks the Lord to cleanse the congregation of hidden wickedness... I know he's talking directly to me. And the choir, when they sing those certain lines about facing judgment or bearing the weight of our transgressions... it's all coordinated. I know they are really warning me. They're trying to tell me, in the only way they can during a holy service, that they know God has marked me. \n\nIt's just so heavy, sitting there in my usual spot—third row from the back, on the aisle, where I've sat since my husband was alive—holding my little paper bulletin and just feeling it all wash over me. The whole church is suffering right now, and they know exactly why. They know I brought this on us. They know the sickness and the bad luck came from the rot I let into my heart. So I really couldn't tell you if anyone else thinks their own mind can do this, but they certainly know mine did. They're just too polite, or maybe too frightened of the mark God put on me, to come right out and say it to my face during coffee hour in the fellowship hall. So they do it through the prayers and the hymns instead. They warn me. And I just have to sit there and listen to it, because they're right.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that Pastor Miller and the choir are not actually sending you messages through their prayers and hymns?\n\nPatient: Possible? No... no, doctor, I don't think that's possible at all. I mean, I know how it might sound to someone who isn't sitting right there in the sanctuary with me, but if you were there, you'd see it just as clearly as I do. \n\nYou see, when Pastor Miller steps up to the pulpit—it's this beautiful old oak pulpit, my husband actually helped sand and varnish it back in the late nineties before his heart gave out, so I know every grain of wood on that thing—when he steps up there and the whole room gets real quiet, you can just feel the shift in the air. And when the pastor says the prayers, he lowers his voice in this very particular way. He talks about cleansing the hidden rot, and the suffering of the flock, and he pauses. And in that pause, I just know. I know in my very bones. \n\nAnd it's not just him. When the choir stands up—they wear these heavy maroon robes, they just got new ones last Easter because the old ones were fraying at the hems—when they stand up and sing those certain lines about facing judgment and the heavy weight of our transgressions... it's not a coincidence. It's just not. I know they are really warning me. They're warning me that God has marked me, plain as day. \n\nThey have to do it that way, don't you see? They can't just stop the service and point a finger at me, so they use the hymns and the prayers. But the message is loud and clear. They know, just like I know, that the church is suffering right now because I brought this on us. All the trouble folks are having, the sickness going around the congregation... I brought that right through the front doors of the church because of what's inside me. So, no, it's not just my imagination playing tricks on me. When they sing and when he prays, it's a warning for me. It has to be. Convince me? Oh, doctor... no. I just... I don't see how anyone on this earth could possibly do that. I mean, my daughter, she certainly tries. They're just too polite to ask me to leave the sanctuary, but they are warning me. They know I'm marked by God for what I did to my friend, and they know my thoughts are poisoning everything around me. They absolutely know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your thoughts might not be the cause of the bad things happening to others?\n\nPatient: Well... no, doctor. No, I don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I know you're trying to help, and my daughter says the same thing. She tells me, 'Mom, you're just grieving, you're just tired from work.' And I am tired, I won't deny that. Working the register at seventy-four is no picnic, let me tell you. My hands ache so much by the time I get home that I can barely open a jar of applesauce for my dinner. But being tired doesn't make you blind to the truth. \n\nI see the truth every Sunday. It's not just a feeling I have in my head, it's right there in front of me. When Pastor Miller stands up at the pulpit... I told you about this, he's such a good man, but he has a responsibility to his flock. When he says those prayers, when he talks about the weight of sin and the consequences of a hardened heart... he's not just speaking generally to the congregation. He's looking right out, and his voice changes just a fraction, and I know he's warning me. He's letting me know that God has marked me. He has to do it from the pulpit because, well, how do you pull an old widow aside and tell her she's destroying the church? \n\nAnd the choir... oh, the choir. It's so beautiful, usually. Mrs. Higgins directs them, she used to teach music at the middle school before she retired. But now, when they sing certain lines... like last week, that hymn about bearing our sins and griefs. The way they held those notes, the way the sopranos' voices just swelled up on those specific words... it was a message. It was a direct message to me. They were warning me, just like the pastor. They know that the church is suffering, that Mary Peters is sick and the van broke down and all these terrible things are happening, because I brought this on us. I brought this rot into the sanctuary. So, no, doctor. It's not possible that I'm mistaken. The signs are everywhere, and they are all pointing right at me. God has marked me for what I did to my friend, and everyone at church knows it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to stop thinking about these ugly thoughts, even when you want to?\n\nPatient: Well... I don't know if \"unable to stop\" is the right way to put it. I'm not really trying to stop them, doctor. Like I said before, I'm not trying to push them away or focus on other things. I mean, how can you stop thinking about something that's just... the truth? It's not like a song stuck in your head, you know? Like when they play those jingles on the radio at the grocery store—they play the same six songs on a loop all day long, and sometimes you just want to turn it off, but you can't. It's not like that. \n\nThese thoughts... they're just my reality now. They're just there. When I wake up in the morning, and my joints are all stiff, and I have to sit on the edge of the bed for a good ten minutes just rubbing my knees before I can even stand up to go make my tea... the thoughts are there. And when I'm making my tea—I always have Earl Grey, with just a little splash of milk, the way my husband used to like it before he passed, God rest his soul—I'm not standing there thinking, \"Oh, I wish I could stop thinking about what I did to my friend.\" I'm just... existing with it. It's like a heavy wet blanket I'm wearing all the time. \n\nSo I don't know if I'm \"unable\" to stop, because I don't think I'm trying to stop. I deserve to feel this way. I deserve the weight of it. Why would I try to stop thinking about it when it's my punishment? It's what God wants for me, clearly. That's why He marked me. That's why Pastor Miller looks at me the way he does. You don't just turn off a punishment from God because it's uncomfortable. You bear it. You just... bear it. So, no, I don't feel like I'm trying to stop and failing. I just... I just let them be there, because they have to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty or ashamed about things that have nothing to do with your friend's death or the church?\n\nPatient: Other things? Well... no. No, doctor, there isn't really room in my head for anything else, because this... this takes up every waking moment. I don't know why I would feel guilty about, oh, leaving the porch light on or forgetting to water the geraniums, when I have this terrible, crushing weight on my soul. \n\nI keep telling them—I tell my daughter, I even tried to tell Mrs. Higgins after service one day, though of course she already knew—I keep telling them that I'm the reason my friend died. It's just a fact, plain as day. She called me, you see, and I was just so tired from standing on my feet all day at the store, scanning barcodes and bagging groceries until my shoulders ached, and I just... I didn't call her back. I looked right at the phone and I didn't pick it up. And I had these ugly thoughts sometimes, just terrible, selfish thoughts because I was tired and I didn't want to hear her complain about her hip again. Just ugly, ugly thoughts inside my head. \n\nAnd then she was gone. And you can't undo that, doctor. You can't just apologize to a gravestone and expect it to wipe the slate clean. God sees what's in your heart. And because of that, because of the rot I let into my soul, I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church. He's punishing the whole congregation because of me. The sickness, the trouble they've been having... it's all flowing out from what I did, from those ugly thoughts and that phone call I never made. So, no, I don't feel ashamed about other little everyday things. How could I even think about anything else, when I know I've brought all this misery down on everyone's heads?\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else believes that their thoughts can cause bad things to happen to others in the same way you do?\n\nPatient: Other people? You mean, do other people think their own thoughts cause harm? Well... I suppose I don't really know what goes on in anyone else's head, doctor. I only know what's in mine, and... well, I know what they believe about me. I don't know if Mrs. Gable or anyone else sitting in the pews thinks they have this awful, destructive power inside them. But I know for an absolute fact that they believe *my* thoughts did this. I know that they know. \n\nLike I was trying to explain to you a few minutes ago about the Sunday services... it's not just my imagination. When Pastor Miller is up there at the altar, and he bows his head and says the prayers for the sick and the afflicted, or when he asks the Lord to cleanse the congregation of hidden wickedness... I know he's talking directly to me. And the choir, when they sing those certain lines about facing judgment or bearing the weight of our transgressions... it's all coordinated. I know they are really warning me. They're trying to tell me, in the only way they can during a holy service, that they know God has marked me. \n\nIt's just so heavy, sitting there in my usual spot—third row from the back, on the aisle, where I've sat since my husband was alive—holding my little paper bulletin and just feeling it all wash over me. The whole church is suffering right now, and they know exactly why. They know I brought this on us. They know the sickness and the bad luck came from the rot I let into my heart. So I really couldn't tell you if anyone else thinks their own mind can do this, but they certainly know mine did. They're just too polite, or maybe too frightened of the mark God put on me, to come right out and say it to my face during coffee hour in the fellowship hall. So they do it through the prayers and the hymns instead. They warn me. And I just have to sit there and listen to it, because they're right.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that Pastor Miller and the choir are not actually sending you messages through their prayers and hymns?\n\nPatient: Possible? No... no, doctor, I don't think that's possible at all. I mean, I know how it might sound to someone who isn't sitting right there in the sanctuary with me, but if you were there, you'd see it just as clearly as I do. \n\nYou see, when Pastor Miller steps up to the pulpit—it's this beautiful old oak pulpit, my husband actually helped sand and varnish it back in the late nineties before his heart gave out, so I know every grain of wood on that thing—when he steps up there and the whole room gets real quiet, you can just feel the shift in the air. And when the pastor says the prayers, he lowers his voice in this very particular way. He talks about cleansing the hidden rot, and the suffering of the flock, and he pauses. And in that pause, I just know. I know in my very bones. \n\nAnd it's not just him. When the choir stands up—they wear these heavy maroon robes, they just got new ones last Easter because the old ones were fraying at the hems—when they stand up and sing those certain lines about facing judgment and the heavy weight of our transgressions... it's not a coincidence. It's just not. I know they are really warning me. They're warning me that God has marked me, plain as day. \n\nThey have to do it that way, don't you see? They can't just stop the service and point a finger at me, so they use the hymns and the prayers. But the message is loud and clear. They know, just like I know, that the church is suffering right now because I brought this on us. All the trouble folks are having, the sickness going around the congregation... I brought that right through the front doors of the church because of what's inside me. So, no, it's not just my imagination playing tricks on me. When they sing and when he prays, it's a warning for me. It has to be. How could it be anything else when the proof is right there in the way everyone is suffering?\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's anything that could happen or anyone who could convince you that your thoughts didn't cause your friend's death or the troubles at church?\n\nPatient: Convince me? Oh, doctor... no. I just... I don't see how anyone on this earth could possibly do that. I mean, my daughter, she certainly tries. She comes over to the house—usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, and she sits right down at my kitchen table, the one with the little yellow floral tablecloth that I bought at Penney's years and years ago—and she holds my hands and tells me it's not my fault. But she's just trying to be a good daughter, bless her heart. She doesn't understand. \n\nBecause... well, like I've been trying to explain to you, the proof is just so undeniable. I know I keep coming back to this, I know I must sound like a broken record to you by now, but how could anyone ever talk me out of it when I sit there every single Sunday and hear it for myself? When the pastor says those prayers, or when the choir sings those certain lines... I just know they are really warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. It's a mark I carry everywhere now, even when I'm just standing there ringing up soup cans at the register. \n\nAnd all those nice people at the church, they're suffering so much right now, and I know it's because I brought this on us. I brought that rot right into the sanctuary with me. Change my mind? Well... I just, I don't see how that would even be possible, doctor. I can feel it. \n\nThey know my thoughts are causing all this misery. It's so clear to me during the service. When Pastor Miller stands up there at the pulpit—he's a good man, Pastor Miller, he's been with us for about twelve years now, came all the way from a parish in Ohio—when he says the prayers, he looks right out over the congregation, but I know he's looking at me. And the words he chooses... he'll talk about repenting for hidden sins, or the weight of a guilty conscience, and I just know. I know he's warning me. He's telling me that God has marked me. \n\nAnd the choir, too. Last week they sang 'Lord, Who Throughout These Forty Days,' and when they got to the part about 'our sins and griefs to bear,' the sopranos... they just held that note, and I could feel it piercing right through me. It wasn't just a hymn, doctor. It was a message. They were singing those certain lines to let me know that they understand why Mary Peters is sick, and why the van broke down, and why the church is suffering. They know I brought this on us. They're just too polite to ask me to leave the sanctuary, but they are warning me. They know I'm marked by God for what I did to my friend, and they know my thoughts are poisoning everything around me. They absolutely know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your thoughts might not be the cause of the bad things happening to others?\n\nPatient: Well... no, doctor. No, I don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I know you're trying to help, and my daughter says the same thing. She tells me, 'Mom, you're just grieving, you're just tired from work.' And I am tired, I won't deny that. Working the register at seventy-four is no picnic, let me tell you. My hands ache so much by the time I get home that I can barely open a jar of applesauce for my dinner. But being tired doesn't make you blind to the truth. \n\nI see the truth every Sunday. It's not just a feeling I have in my head, it's right there in front of me. When Pastor Miller stands up at the pulpit... I told you about this, he's such a good man, but he has a responsibility to his flock. When he says those prayers, when he talks about the weight of sin and the consequences of a hardened heart... he's not just speaking generally to the congregation. He's looking right out, and his voice changes just a fraction, and I know he's warning me. He's letting me know that God has marked me. He has to do it from the pulpit because, well, how do you pull an old widow aside and tell her she's destroying the church? \n\nAnd the choir... oh, the choir. It's so beautiful, usually. Mrs. Higgins directs them, she used to teach music at the middle school before she retired. But now, when they sing certain lines... like last week, that hymn about bearing our sins and griefs. The way they held those notes, the way the sopranos' voices just swelled up on those specific words... it was a message. It was a direct message to me. They were warning me, just like the pastor. They know that the church is suffering, that Mary Peters is sick and the van broke down and all these terrible things are happening, because I brought this on us. I brought this rot into the sanctuary. So, no, doctor. It's not possible that I'm mistaken. The signs are everywhere, and they are all pointing right at me. God has marked me for what I did to my friend, and everyone at church knows it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to stop thinking about these ugly thoughts, even when you want to?\n\nPatient: Well... I don't know if \"unable to stop\" is the right way to put it. I'm not really trying to stop them, doctor. Like I said before, I'm not trying to push them away or focus on other things. I mean, how can you stop thinking about something that's just... the truth? It's not like a song stuck in your head, you know? Like when they play those jingles on the radio at the grocery store—they play the same six songs on a loop all day long, and sometimes you just want to turn it off, but you can't. It's not like that. \n\nThese thoughts... they're just my reality now. They're just there. When I wake up in the morning, and my joints are all stiff, and I have to sit on the edge of the bed for a good ten minutes just rubbing my knees before I can even stand up to go make my tea... the thoughts are there. And when I'm making my tea—I always have Earl Grey, with just a little splash of milk, the way my husband used to like it before he passed, God rest his soul—I'm not standing there thinking, \"Oh, I wish I could stop thinking about what I did to my friend.\" I'm just... existing with it. It's like a heavy wet blanket I'm wearing all the time. \n\nSo I don't know if I'm \"unable\" to stop, because I don't think I'm trying to stop. I deserve to feel this way. I deserve the weight of it. Why would I try to stop thinking about it when it's my punishment? It's what God wants for me, clearly. That's why He marked me. That's why Pastor Miller looks at me the way he does. You don't just turn off a punishment from God because it's uncomfortable. You bear it. You just... bear it. So, no, I don't feel like I'm trying to stop and failing. I just... I just let them be there, because they have to be.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty or ashamed about things that have nothing to do with your friend's death or the church?\n\nPatient: Other things? Well... no. No, doctor, there isn't really room in my head for anything else, because this... this takes up every waking moment. I don't know why I would feel guilty about, oh, leaving the porch light on or forgetting to water the geraniums, when I have this terrible, crushing weight on my soul. \n\nI keep telling them—I tell my daughter, I even tried to tell Mrs. Higgins after service one day, though of course she already knew—I keep telling them that I'm the reason my friend died. It's just a fact, plain as day. She called me, you see, and I was just so tired from standing on my feet all day at the store, scanning barcodes and bagging groceries until my shoulders ached, and I just... I didn't call her back. I looked right at the phone and I didn't pick it up. And I had these ugly thoughts sometimes, just terrible, selfish thoughts because I was tired and I didn't want to hear her complain about her hip again. Just ugly, ugly thoughts inside my head. \n\nAnd then she was gone. And you can't undo that, doctor. You can't just apologize to a gravestone and expect it to wipe the slate clean. God sees what's in your heart. And because of that, because of the rot I let into my soul, I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church. He's punishing the whole congregation because of me. The sickness, the trouble they've been having... it's all flowing out from what I did, from those ugly thoughts and that phone call I never made. So, no, I don't feel ashamed about other little everyday things. How could I even think about anything else, when I know I've brought all this misery down on everyone's heads?\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else believes that their thoughts can cause bad things to happen to others in the same way you do?\n\nPatient: Other people? You mean, do other people think their own thoughts cause harm? Well... I suppose I don't really know what goes on in anyone else's head, doctor. I only know what's in mine, and... well, I know what they believe about me. I don't know if Mrs. Gable or anyone else sitting in the pews thinks they have this awful, destructive power inside them. But I know for an absolute fact that they believe *my* thoughts did this. I know that they know. \n\nLike I was trying to explain to you a few minutes ago about the Sunday services... it's not just my imagination. When Pastor Miller is up there at the altar, and he bows his head and says the prayers for the sick and the afflicted, or when he asks the Lord to cleanse the congregation of hidden wickedness... I know he's talking directly to me. And the choir, when they sing those certain lines about facing judgment or bearing the weight of our transgressions... it's all coordinated. I know they are really warning me. They're trying to tell me, in the only way they can during a holy service, that they know God has marked me. \n\nIt's just so heavy, sitting there in my usual spot—third row from the back, on the aisle, where I've sat since my husband was alive—holding my little paper bulletin and just feeling it all wash over me. The whole church is suffering right now, and they know exactly why. They know I brought this on us. They know the sickness and the bad luck came from the rot I let into my heart. So I really couldn't tell you if anyone else thinks their own mind can do this, but they certainly know mine did. They're just too polite, or maybe too frightened of the mark God put on me, to come right out and say it to my face during coffee hour in the fellowship hall. So they do it through the prayers and the hymns instead. They warn me. And I just have to sit there and listen to it, because they're right.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that Pastor Miller and the choir are not actually sending you messages through their prayers and hymns?\n\nPatient: Possible? No... no, doctor, I don't think that's possible at all. And when the pastor says the prayers, he lowers his voice in this very particular way. He talks about cleansing the hidden rot, and the suffering of the flock, and he pauses. And in that pause, I just know. I know in my very bones. \n\nAnd it's not just him. When the choir stands up—they wear these heavy maroon robes, they just got new ones last Easter because the old ones were fraying at the hems—when they stand up and sing those certain lines about facing judgment and the heavy weight of our transgressions... it's not a coincidence. It's just not. I know they are really warning me. They're warning me that God has marked me, plain as day. \n\nThey have to do it that way, don't you see? They can't just stop the service and point a finger at me, so they use the hymns and the prayers. But the message is loud and clear. They know, just like I know, that the church is suffering right now because I brought this on us. All the trouble folks are having, the sickness going around the congregation... I brought that right through the front doors of the church because of what's inside me. So, no, it's not just my imagination playing tricks on me. When they sing and when he prays, it's a warning for me. It has to be. How could it be anything else when the proof is right there in the way everyone is suffering?\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's anything that could happen or anyone who could convince you that your thoughts didn't cause your friend's death or the troubles at church?\n\nPatient: Convince me? Oh, doctor... no. I just... I don't see how anyone on this earth could possibly do that. I mean, my daughter, she certainly tries. She comes over to the house—usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, and she sits right down at my kitchen table, the one with the little yellow floral tablecloth that I bought at Penney's years and years ago—and she holds my hands and tells me it's not my fault. But she's just trying to be a good daughter, bless her heart. She doesn't understand. \n\nBecause... well, like I've been trying to explain to you, the proof is just so undeniable. I know I keep coming back to this, I know I must sound like a broken record to you by now, but how could anyone ever talk me out of it when I sit there every single Sunday and hear it for myself? When the pastor says those prayers, or when the choir sings those certain lines... I just know they are really warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. It's a mark I carry everywhere now, even when I'm just standing there ringing up soup cans at the register. \n\nAnd all those nice people at the church, they're suffering so much right now, and I know it's because I brought this on us. I brought that rot right into the sanctuary with me. They'd have to make the pastor say something different. But he doesn't. He talks about the hidden wickedness, and the choir sings about judgment, and I know exactly who they mean. So no, doctor, there's no talking me out of the plain truth.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible for you to ever change your mind about your thoughts causing harm to others?\n\nPatient: Change my mind? Well... I just, I don't see how that would even be possible, doctor. Intrusive? Well... I don't know if that's the right word for it, doctor. It's not like... it's not like a song that gets stuck in your head, you know, like when they play those old Christmas jingles over the loudspeakers at the grocery store starting right after Thanksgiving, and you just can't stop humming them even when you're trying to sleep. Anyone else? Oh, doctor, I... I really couldn't speak for anyone else in the whole world. I don't know how other people's minds work, I really don't. I just know what happened with me, and I just know the burden I have to wake up with every single morning.

Incorrect? Oh, doctor... I just... I don't see how that could be. I really don't. I know you doctors have to ask these things, you have to look at all the angles and make sure a person's mind is working right, but... well, you have to understand, I've been going to that same church for forty-two years. Forty-two years this coming Easter. My late husband and I, we sat in the third pew on the left every single Sunday, right behind the Miller family, back when their children were still small enough to fidget through the sermon. I know that church. I know the way the light comes through the stained glass window of St. Jude right around eleven-fifteen, and I know exactly how Pastor Evans—God rest his soul—used to preach, and I know exactly how the new pastor, Pastor Miller, does it now.

So when I tell you about the prayers... it's not a misunderstanding. It's not me just getting confused in my old age. When Pastor Miller stands up there, right after the announcements about the bake sale or the youth group car wash, and he bows his head and starts the intercessory prayer... there's a shift. The tone of his voice changes. And he says these specific words, these phrases about 'hidden sins' and 'a rot within the congregation.' He never used to say those things. Never. Not until my friend died. Not until I let those ugly thoughts take over and I didn't answer that phone. 

And the choir! Oh, the choir... Mrs. Gable has been directing them for fifteen years, and she always preferred the upbeat, joyful hymns. But now? Now, right as I'm sitting there, trying to make myself as small as possible in that third pew, they sing these heavy, mournful lines. 'Though your sins be as scarlet,' they sing, and 'The Lord's judgment is upon the wicked.' And the way they look... they don't look right at me, no, they're too polite for that, but I can feel it. I know they are warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. 

How could I misinterpret that? It's as plain as the nametag on my grocery store uniform. God put a mark on me for what I did, for the thoughts that killed my friend, and now the whole church is suffering because I brought this curse right through the front doors and down the center aisle. I brought it on us. So, no, doctor... I don't think I'm incorrect. I wish I was. Lord, I wish I was just a crazy old woman making things up. But when they say those prayers and sing those lines... they know. And they're making sure I know, too.

They know, just like I know, that the church is suffering right now because I brought this on us. All the trouble folks are having, the sickness going around the congregation... I brought that right through the front doors of the church because of what's inside me. So, no, it's not just my imagination playing tricks on me. When they sing and when he prays, it's a warning for me. It has to be. How could it be anything else when the proof is right there in the way everyone is suffering?\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's anything that could happen or anyone who could convince you that your thoughts didn't cause your friend's death or the troubles at church?\n\nPatient: Convince me? Oh, doctor... no. I just... I don't see how anyone on this earth could possibly do that. I mean, my daughter, she certainly tries. She comes over to the house—usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, and she sits right down at my kitchen table, the one with the little yellow floral tablecloth that I bought at Penney's years and years ago—and she holds my hands and tells me it's not my fault. But she's just trying to be a good daughter, bless her heart. She doesn't understand. \n\nBecause... well, like I've been trying to explain to you, the proof is just so undeniable. I know I keep coming back to this, I know I must sound like a broken record to you by now, but how could anyone ever talk me out of it when I sit there every single Sunday and hear it for myself? When the pastor says those prayers, or when the choir sings those certain lines... I just know they are really warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. It's a mark I carry everywhere now, even when I'm just standing there ringing up soup cans at the register. \n\nAnd all those nice people at the church, they're suffering so much right now, and I know it's because I brought this on us. I brought that rot right into the sanctuary with me. So, if someone wanted to convince me that my thoughts didn't cause all this... well, they'd have to change what I hear with my own two ears during the service. They'd have to make the pastor say something different. But he doesn't. He talks about the hidden wickedness, and the choir sings about judgment, and I know exactly who they mean. So no, doctor, there's no talking me out of the plain truth.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible for you to ever change your mind about your thoughts causing harm to others?\n\nPatient: Change my mind? Well... I just, I don't see how that would even be possible, doctor. I know I keep bringing up the church, and I probably sound like an old woman who just can't let a thing go, but... well, when you've been sitting in those same pews for over forty years, you just know when things change. You know the rhythms of it. \n\nSo when the pastor says the prayers—especially the long ones right after Mr. Henderson and the other ushers pass the brass offering plates—or when the choir sings certain lines from the hymnal... I mean, I know they are really warning me. It’s not a guess. They are warning me that God has marked me. And how can I just decide to stop believing that when I look around and see that the church is suffering? All those good people having such a hard time, and it’s because I brought this on us. I brought it right in with me. \n\nI would love to change my mind, I really would. It's a terrible, terrible burden to carry, especially when I'm just trying to get through my shift at the store, scanning barcodes and bagging groceries, knowing what I've done and what's inside me. But you can't just wish away the truth. If I could just flip a switch in my brain and pretend it wasn't happening, I'd do it in a heartbeat. But when the whole congregation has to use the Sunday service to warn you about the mark God put on you... well, you can't just change your mind about a thing like that, can you? It's just the reality of what I've done to them.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these thoughts about causing harm to others are intrusive, meaning they enter your mind even when you don't want to think about them?\n\nPatient: Intrusive? Well... I don't know if that's the right word for it, doctor. It's not like... it's not like a song that gets stuck in your head, you know, like when they play those old Christmas jingles over the loudspeakers at the grocery store starting right after Thanksgiving, and you just can't stop humming them even when you're trying to sleep. It's not like that. \n\nIt's just... it's just the truth of what's happening. I don't sit around trying to think about how I brought this rot into the church, if that's what you mean. Lord knows I'd rather think about anything else. I try to focus on my work, making sure I don't double-scan the produce or accidentally squish the bread when I'm bagging for Mrs. Higgins—she's awfully particular about her bread, always buys that soft white kind with the blue wrapper. But even when I'm standing there, trying so hard just to do my job and be a normal person, I just know. \n\nI know what I am. I know what I've done. It's not a thought that just pops in out of nowhere to bother me, it's just... it's just reality. It's like knowing the sky is blue or knowing my husband is gone. I don't have to want to think about it for it to be true. And then Sunday rolls around, and I go to service, and I hear the pastor's prayers, and the choir sings those hymns... and there it is, plain as day, staring me right in the face. They're warning me. So, no, I wouldn't say they're intrusive thoughts, doctor. I'd just say it's the terrible, heavy truth of my life now, and it's there whether I want to look at it or not.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that anyone else could possibly believe that their thoughts alone caused someone's death?\n\nPatient: Anyone else? Oh, doctor, I... I really couldn't speak for anyone else in the whole world. I don't know how other people's minds work, I really don't. I just know what happened with me, and I just know the burden I have to wake up with every single morning. \n\nI keep telling them—I keep telling my daughter when she comes over, and I even tried to tell Pastor Miller when he came by to check on me that one afternoon, though he just sighed and patted my hand—I keep telling them that I’m the reason my friend died. My dear friend. She... well, she called me, you see. It was right before I had to put my uniform on and pin my nametag to my collar for the afternoon shift at the store. The phone just rang and rang, and I sat there at the kitchen table looking at it. I didn’t call her back. I just let it ring because... well, because sometimes I had these ugly thoughts. Just awful, wicked, ugly thoughts inside me that I can't even bear to repeat, and I let those thoughts take over instead of picking up the receiver like a good Christian woman should. \n\nAnd then she passed. And it was my thoughts that did it. The ugliness in me, reaching out and causing it. I know you're trying to ask if it makes sense, if anyone else could believe such a thing, but when you live with it... when you know for an absolute fact it's your fault... it's not just a belief. \n\nAnd it didn't stop with her, either. Like I've been trying to tell you, it spread. I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church because of me. All those good people in the congregation, suffering, and it's because the Lord sees exactly what I did. He sees those ugly thoughts I had, and He knows I didn't pick up that phone, and now He's bringing His judgment down on the whole sanctuary just to get to me. So I don't know if anyone else could believe it, doctor. I really don't. But I don't have the luxury of just wondering about it. I have to live with knowing I caused it all.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of the pastor's prayers and the choir's songs is incorrect?\n\nPatient: Incorrect? Oh, doctor... I just... I don't see how that could be. I really don't. I know you doctors have to ask these things, you have to look at all the angles and make sure a person's mind is working right, but... well, you have to understand, I've been going to that same church for forty-two years. Forty-two years this coming Easter. My late husband and I, we sat in the third pew on the left every single Sunday, right behind the Miller family, back when their children were still small enough to fidget through the sermon. I know that church. I know the way the light comes through the stained glass window of St. Jude right around eleven-fifteen, and I know exactly how Pastor Evans—God rest his soul—used to preach, and I know exactly how the new pastor, Pastor Miller, does it now.\n\nSo when I tell you about the prayers... it's not a misunderstanding. It's not me just getting confused in my old age. When Pastor Miller stands up there, right after the announcements about the bake sale or the youth group car wash, and he bows his head and starts the intercessory prayer... there's a shift. The tone of his voice changes. And he says these specific words, these phrases about 'hidden sins' and 'a rot within the congregation.' He never used to say those things. Never. Not until my friend died. Not until I let those ugly thoughts take over and I didn't answer that phone. \n\nAnd the choir! Oh, the choir... Mrs. Gable has been directing them for fifteen years, and she always preferred the upbeat, joyful hymns. But now? Now, right as I'm sitting there, trying to make myself as small as possible in that third pew, they sing these heavy, mournful lines. 'Though your sins be as scarlet,' they sing, and 'The Lord's judgment is upon the wicked.' And the way they look... they don't look right at me, no, they're too polite for that, but I can feel it. I know they are warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. \n\nHow could I misinterpret that? It's as plain as the nametag on my grocery store uniform. God put a mark on me for what I did, for the thoughts that killed my friend, and now the whole church is suffering because I brought this curse right through the front doors and down the center aisle. Evidence? Oh, doctor... what kind of evidence could there possibly be? A piece of paper? Somebody's signature on a form? No... no, there isn't anything in this world, no earthly proof that could ever make me un-see what is happening right in front of my face. 

I know I keep going on and on about this, and I know I've already told you about Sunday mornings, but you have to understand that what happens there *is* my evidence. When the pastor says the prayers—those deep, heavy prayers right before Mr. Henderson and his teenage grandson pass the brass offering plates down the aisles—or when the choir sings those certain lines... I know they are really warning me. It's not a guess, doctor, and it's not just my imagination playing tricks on an old woman. I know they are warning me that God has marked me. 

How could any evidence you have here in this clinic outweigh that? You can't show me a medical chart or a psychology book that explains away the reality of what I've done. The church is suffering. It is truly suffering, falling apart right before our eyes, and it is because I brought this on us with the wickedness inside me. The evidence is the punishment itself. God put a mark on my soul for what I did to my dear friend, for letting those awful thoughts kill her while I just sat there staring at the telephone on my kitchen table, dreading my shift at the store. 

So, no. I'm sorry, but no. There is absolutely no evidence that could ever change my mind, because I have to live inside the evidence every single day. I have to wake up with it, I have to carry it with me to the cash register, and I have to carry it into that third pew, knowing I ruined everything and that they all know it, too.

He heard what was in my mind, and He acted on it. A person whose own selfishness kills their friend... that is a rotten person. There's no other word for it. They know I'm a widow and I work hard, so they smile and they hand me the bulletin on Sunday mornings. But... but I know they know. I can see it. I can feel it. \n\nThey know my thoughts are causing all this misery. It's so clear to me during the service. They absolutely know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your thoughts might not be the cause of the bad things happening to others?\n\nPatient: Well... no, doctor. No, I don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I know you're trying to help, and my daughter says the same thing. She tells me, 'Mom, you're just grieving, you're just tired from work.' I told you about this, he's such a good man, but he has a responsibility to his flock. When he says those prayers, when he talks about the weight of sin and the consequences of a hardened heart... he's not just speaking generally to the congregation. When the choir stands up—they wear these heavy maroon robes, they just got new ones last Easter because the old ones were fraying at the hems—when they stand up and sing those certain lines about facing judgment and the heavy weight of our transgressions... it's not a coincidence. It's just not. I know they are really warning me. They're warning me that God has marked me, plain as day. \n\nThey have to do it that way, don't you see? They can't just stop the service and point a finger at me, so they use the hymns and the prayers. But the message is loud and clear. They know, just like I know, that the church is suffering right now because I brought this on us. All the trouble folks are having, the sickness going around the congregation... I brought that right through the front doors of the church because of what's inside me. So, no, it's not just my imagination playing tricks on me. When they sing and when he prays, it's a warning for me. It has to be. How could it be anything else when the proof is right there in the way everyone is suffering?\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's anything that could happen or anyone who could convince you that your thoughts didn't cause your friend's death or the troubles at church?\n\nPatient: Convince me? Oh, doctor... no. I just... I don't see how anyone on this earth could possibly do that. I mean, my daughter, she certainly tries. She comes over to the house—usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, and she sits right down at my kitchen table, the one with the little yellow floral tablecloth that I bought at Penney's years and years ago—and she holds my hands and tells me it's not my fault. But she's just trying to be a good daughter, bless her heart. She doesn't understand. \n\nBecause... well, like I've been trying to explain to you, the proof is just so undeniable. I know I keep coming back to this, I know I must sound like a broken record to you by now, but how could anyone ever talk me out of it when I sit there every single Sunday and hear it for myself? When the pastor says those prayers, or when the choir sings those certain lines... I just know they are really warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. It's a mark I carry everywhere now, even when I'm just standing there ringing up soup cans at the register. \n\nAnd all those nice people at the church, they're suffering so much right now, and I know it's because I brought this on us. I brought that rot right into the sanctuary with me. So, if someone wanted to convince me that my thoughts didn't cause all this... well, they'd have to change what I hear with my own two ears during the service. They'd have to make the pastor say something different. But he doesn't. He talks about the hidden wickedness, and the choir sings about judgment, and I know exactly who they mean. So no, doctor, there's no talking me out of the plain truth.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible for you to ever change your mind about your thoughts causing harm to others?\n\nPatient: Change my mind? Well... I just, I don't see how that would even be possible, doctor. I know I keep bringing up the church, and I probably sound like an old woman who just can't let a thing go, but... well, when you've been sitting in those same pews for over forty years, you just know when things change. You know the rhythms of it. \n\nSo when the pastor says the prayers—especially the long ones right after Mr. Henderson and the other ushers pass the brass offering plates—or when the choir sings certain lines from the hymnal... I mean, I know they are really warning me. It’s not a guess. They are warning me that God has marked me. And how can I just decide to stop believing that when I look around and see that the church is suffering? All those good people having such a hard time, and it’s because I brought this on us. I brought it right in with me. \n\nI would love to change my mind, I really would. It's a terrible, terrible burden to carry, especially when I'm just trying to get through my shift at the store, scanning barcodes and bagging groceries, knowing what I've done and what's inside me. But you can't just wish away the truth. If I could just flip a switch in my brain and pretend it wasn't happening, I'd do it in a heartbeat. But when the whole congregation has to use the Sunday service to warn you about the mark God put on you... well, you can't just change your mind about a thing like that, can you? It's just the reality of what I've done to them.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these thoughts about causing harm to others are intrusive, meaning they enter your mind even when you don't want to think about them?\n\nPatient: Intrusive? Well... I don't know if that's the right word for it, doctor. I'd just say it's the terrible, heavy truth of my life now, and it's there whether I want to look at it or not.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that anyone else could possibly believe that their thoughts alone caused someone's death?\n\nPatient: Anyone else? Oh, doctor, I... I really couldn't speak for anyone else in the whole world. I don't know how other people's minds work, I really don't. All those good people in the congregation, suffering, and it's because the Lord sees exactly what I did. He sees those ugly thoughts I had, and He knows I didn't pick up that phone, and now He's bringing His judgment down on the whole sanctuary just to get to me. So I don't know if anyone else could believe it, doctor. I really don't. But I don't have the luxury of just wondering about it. I have to live with knowing I caused it all.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of the pastor's prayers and the choir's songs is incorrect?\n\nPatient: Incorrect? Oh, doctor... I just... I don't see how that could be. I really don't. But when the whole congregation has to use the Sunday service to warn you about the mark God put on you... well, you can't just change your mind about a thing like that, can you? It's just the reality of what I've done to them.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these thoughts about causing harm to others are intrusive, meaning they enter your mind even when you don't want to think about them?\n\nPatient: Intrusive? Well... I don't know if that's the right word for it, doctor. It's not like... it's not like a song that gets stuck in your head, you know, like when they play those old Christmas jingles over the loudspeakers at the grocery store starting right after Thanksgiving, and you just can't stop humming them even when you're trying to sleep. It's not like that. \n\nIt's just... it's just the truth of what's happening. I don't sit around trying to think about how I brought this rot into the church, if that's what you mean. Lord knows I'd rather think about anything else. I try to focus on my work, making sure I don't double-scan the produce or accidentally squish the bread when I'm bagging for Mrs. Higgins—she's awfully particular about her bread, always buys that soft white kind with the blue wrapper. But even when I'm standing there, trying so hard just to do my job and be a normal person, I just know. \n\nI know what I am. I know what I've done. It's not a thought that just pops in out of nowhere to bother me, it's just... it's just reality. It's like knowing the sky is blue or knowing my husband is gone. I don't have to want to think about it for it to be true. And then Sunday rolls around, and I go to service, and I hear the pastor's prayers, and the choir sings those hymns... and there it is, plain as day, staring me right in the face. They're warning me. So, no, I wouldn't say they're intrusive thoughts, doctor. I'd just say it's the terrible, heavy truth of my life now, and it's there whether I want to look at it or not.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that anyone else could possibly believe that their thoughts alone caused someone's death?\n\nPatient: Anyone else? Oh, doctor, I... I really couldn't speak for anyone else in the whole world. I don't know how other people's minds work, I really don't. I just know what happened with me, and I just know the burden I have to wake up with every single morning. \n\nI keep telling them—I keep telling my daughter when she comes over, and I even tried to tell Pastor Miller when he came by to check on me that one afternoon, though he just sighed and patted my hand—I keep telling them that I’m the reason my friend died. My dear friend. She... well, she called me, you see. It was right before I had to put my uniform on and pin my nametag to my collar for the afternoon shift at the store. The phone just rang and rang, and I sat there at the kitchen table looking at it. I didn’t call her back. I just let it ring because... well, because sometimes I had these ugly thoughts. Just awful, wicked, ugly thoughts inside me that I can't even bear to repeat, and I let those thoughts take over instead of picking up the receiver like a good Christian woman should. \n\nAnd then she passed. And it was my thoughts that did it. The ugliness in me, reaching out and causing it. I know you're trying to ask if it makes sense, if anyone else could believe such a thing, but when you live with it... when you know for an absolute fact it's your fault... it's not just a belief. \n\nAnd it didn't stop with her, either. Like I've been trying to tell you, it spread. I know the Lord is punishing everybody at church because of me. All those good people in the congregation, suffering, and it's because the Lord sees exactly what I did. He sees those ugly thoughts I had, and He knows I didn't pick up that phone, and now He's bringing His judgment down on the whole sanctuary just to get to me. So I don't know if anyone else could believe it, doctor. I really don't. But I don't have the luxury of just wondering about it. I have to live with knowing I caused it all.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of the pastor's prayers and the choir's songs is incorrect?\n\nPatient: Incorrect? Oh, doctor... I just... I don't see how that could be. I really don't.
