Forty-two years this coming Easter. My late husband and I, we sat in the third pew on the left every single Sunday, right behind the Miller family, back when their children were still small enough to fidget through the sermon. I know that church. I know the way the light comes through the stained glass window of St. Jude right around eleven-fifteen, and I know exactly how Pastor Evans—God rest his soul—used to preach, and I know exactly how the new pastor, Pastor Miller, does it now.\n\nSo when I tell you about the prayers... it's not a misunderstanding. It's not me just getting confused in my old age. When Pastor Miller stands up there, right after the announcements about the bake sale or the youth group car wash, and he bows his head and starts the intercessory prayer... there's a shift. The tone of his voice changes. And he says these specific words, these phrases about 'hidden sins' and 'a rot within the congregation.' He never used to say those things. Never. Not until my friend died. Not until I let those ugly thoughts take over and I didn't answer that phone. \n\nAnd the choir! Oh, the choir... Mrs. Gable has been directing them for fifteen years, and she always preferred the upbeat, joyful hymns. But now? Now, right as I'm sitting there, trying to make myself as small as possible in that third pew, they sing these heavy, mournful lines. 'Though your sins be as scarlet,' they sing, and 'The Lord's judgment is upon the wicked.' And the way they look... they don't look right at me, no, they're too polite for that, but I can feel it. I know they are warning me. They are warning me that God has marked me. \n\nHow could I misinterpret that? It's as plain as the nametag on my grocery store uniform. God put a mark on me for what I did, for the thoughts that killed my friend, and now the whole church is suffering because I brought this curse right through the front doors and down the center aisle. I brought it on us. So, no, doctor... I don't think I'm incorrect. I wish I was. Lord, I wish I was just a crazy old woman making things up. But when they say those prayers and sing those lines... they know. I brought it right in with me. \n\nI would love to change my mind, I really would. But when the whole congregation has to use the Sunday service to warn you about the mark God put on you... well, you can't just change your mind about a thing like that, can you? How could I even think about anything else, when I know I've brought all this misery down on everyone's heads?\n\nDoctor: Do you think anyone else believes that their thoughts can cause bad things to happen to others in the same way you do?\n\nPatient: Other people? You mean, do other people think their own thoughts cause harm? Well... I suppose I don't really know what goes on in anyone else's head, doctor. The whole church is suffering right now, and they know exactly why. They know I brought this on us. They know the sickness and the bad luck came from the rot I let into my heart. So I really couldn't tell you if anyone else thinks their own mind can do this, but they certainly know mine did. They're just too polite, or maybe too frightened of the mark God put on me, to come right out and say it to my face during coffee hour in the fellowship hall. No... no, doctor, I don't think that's possible at all. I mean, I know how it might sound to someone who isn't sitting right there in the sanctuary with me, but if you were there, you'd see it just as clearly as I do. \n\nYou see, when Pastor Miller steps up to the pulpit—it's this beautiful old oak pulpit, my husband actually helped sand and varnish it back in the late nineties before his heart gave out, so I know every grain of wood on that thing—when he steps up there and the whole room gets real quiet, you can just feel the shift in the air. When the choir stands up—they wear these heavy maroon robes, they just got new ones last Easter because the old ones were fraying at the hems—when they stand up and sing those certain lines about facing judgment and the heavy weight of our transgressions... it's not a coincidence. It's just not. I know they are really warning me. They're warning me that God has marked me, plain as day. \n\nThey have to do it that way, don't you see? They can't just stop the service and point a finger at me, so they use the hymns and the prayers. But the message is loud and clear. They know, just like I know, that the church is suffering right now because I brought this on us. All the trouble folks are having, the sickness going around the congregation... I brought that right through the front doors of the church because of what's inside me. So, no, it's not just my imagination playing tricks on me. When they sing and when he prays, it's a warning for me. It has to be. How could it be anything else when the proof is right there in the way everyone is suffering?\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's anything that could happen or anyone who could convince you that your thoughts didn't cause your friend's death or the troubles at church?\n\nPatient: Convince me? Oh, doctor... no. I just... I don't see how anyone on this earth could possibly do that. I mean, my daughter, she certainly tries. She comes over to the house—usually on Tuesday evenings after she gets off work, and she sits right down at my kitchen table, the one with the little yellow floral tablecloth that I bought at Penney's years and years ago—and she holds my hands and tells me it's not my fault. But she's just trying to be a good daughter, bless her heart. She doesn't understand. \n\nBecause... well, like I've been trying to explain to you, the proof is just so undeniable. Well... I just, I don't see how that would even be possible, doctor. I know I keep bringing up the church, and I probably sound like an old woman who just can't let a thing go, but... well, when you've been sitting in those same pews for over forty years, you just know when things change. But you can't just wish away the truth. If I could just flip a switch in my brain and pretend it wasn't happening, I'd do it in a heartbeat. It's not like that. \n\nIt's just... it's just the truth of what's happening. I don't sit around trying to think about how I brought this rot into the church, if that's what you mean. Lord knows I'd rather think about anything else. I don't have to want to think about it for it to be true.
